APPENDIX 1: GUIDELINES FOR INTEGRATING COMMUNITY SERVICE LEARNING (CSL)
Introduction
In Grade 8, learners will undertake an integrated Community Service Learning (CSL) project of choice from a single or combined
subject. The CSL project will enable the learner to apply knowledge and skills from other subjects to address a problem in th e
community. The implementation of the integrated CSL project will take a Whole School Approach, where  all members of the
school community including teachers, school administration, parents/guardians/ local community and support staff. It will  be a
collaborative effort where the teacher of Social Studies coordinates and works with other subject teachers to design and implement
the integrated CSL projects.  The teachers will select a theme drawn from different Learning Areas and the broader categories of
Pertinent and Conte mporary Issues (PCIs) for the CSL project.  It should also provide an opportunity for development of core
competencies and nurturing of values. Learners will undertake one common integrated class CSL project following a 6 -step
milestone approach as follows:
Milestone Description
Milestone 1
Problem Identification
Learners study their community to understand the challenges faced and their effects on community
members. Some of the challenges in the community can be:
● Environmental degradation
● Lifestyle diseases, Communicable and non-communicable diseases
● Poverty
● Violence and conflicts in the community
● Food security issues
33
Milestone 2 Designing a solution
Learners create an intervention to address the challenge identified.
Milestone 3 Planning for the Project
Learners share roles, create a list of activities to be undertaken, mobilise resources needed to create their
intervention and set timelines for execution
Milestone 4 Implementation
The learners execute the project and keep evidence of work done.
Milestone 5 Showcasing /Exhibition and Report Writing
Exhibitions involve showcasing learners’ project items to the community and reflecting on the feedback
Learners write a report detailing their project activities and learnings from feedback
Milestone 6 Reflection
Learners review all project work to learn from the challenges faced.
They link project work with academic concepts, noting how the concepts enabled them to do their
project as well as how the project helped to deepen learning of the academic concepts.
NOTE: The milestones will be staggered across the 3 terms of the academic calendar.
34
Assessment of CSL integrated Project
Assessment for the integrated CSL project will be conducted formatively. The assessment will consider both the process and
end product. This entails assessing each of the milestone stages of the integrated CSL class project. It will focus on 3
components namely: skills from various learning areas applied in carrying out the project, core competencies developed and
values nurtured.
35

NATIONAL GOALS OF EDUCATION
Education in Kenya should:
1.  Foster nationalism and patriotism and promote national unity.
Kenya’s people belong to different communities, races and religions, but these differences need not divide them. They must be
able to live and interact as Kenyans. It is a paramount duty of education to help young people acquire this sense of nationho od
by removing conflicts and promoting positive attitudes of mutual respect  which enable them to live together in harmony and
foster patriotism in order to make a positive contribution to the life of the nation.
2.  Promote the social, economic, technological and industrial needs for national development.
Education should prepare the youth of the country to play an effective and productive role in the life of the nation.
a) Social Needs
Education in Kenya must prepare children for changes in attitudes and relationships which are necessary for the
smooth progress of a rapidly devel oping modern economy. There is bound to be a silent social revolution following
the wake of rapid modernisation. Education should assist our youth to adapt to this change.
b) Economic Needs
Education in Kenya should produce citizens with the skills, knowledg e, expertise and personal qualities that are
required to support a growing economy. Kenya is building up a modern and independent economy which is in need of
an adequate and relevant domestic workforce.
c) Technological and Industrial Needs
Education in Kenya should provide learners with the necessary skills and attitudes for industrial development. Kenya
recognises the rapid industrial and technological changes taking place, especially in the developed world. We can only
be part of this development if our ed ucation system is deliberately focused on the knowledge, skills and attitudes that
will prepare our young people for these changing global trends.
iii
3. Promote individual development and self-fulfilment
Education should provide opportunities for the fulle st development of individual talents and personality. It should help
children to develop their potential interests and abilities. A vital aspect of individual development is the building of character.
4. Promote sound moral and religious values.
Education should provide for the development of knowledge, skills and attitudes that will enhance the acquisition of sound
moral values and help children to grow up into self-disciplined, self-reliant and integrated citizens.
5.   Promote social equity and responsibility.
Education should promote social equality and foster a sense of social responsibility within an education system which
provides equal educational opportunities for all. It should give all children varied and challenging opportunities for collec tive
activities and corporate social service irrespective of gender, ability or geographical environment.
6. Promote respect for and development of Kenya’s rich and varied cultures.
Education should instil in the youth of Kenya an understanding of past and present cultures and their valid place in
contemporary society. Children should be able to blend the best of traditional values with the changing requirements that mus t
follow rapid development in order to build a stable and modern society.
7. Promote international consciousness and foster positive attitudes towards other nations.
Kenya is part of the international community. It is part of the complicated and interdependent network of peoples and nations .
Education should therefore lead the youth of the country to accept membership of this international community with all the
obligations and responsibilities, rights and benefits that this membership entails.
8. Promote positive attitudes towards good health and environmental protection.
Education should inculcate in young people the value of good health in order for them to avoid indulging in activities that will
lead to physical or mental ill health. It should foster positive attitudes towards environmental development and conservation. It
should lead the youth of Kenya to appreciate the need for a healthy environment.

LEARNING OUTCOMES FOR JUNIOR SCHOOL
By end of Junior School, the learner should be able to:
1. Apply literacy, numeracy and logical thinking skills for appropriate self-expression.
2. Communicate effectively, verbally and non-verbally, in diverse contexts.
3. Demonstrate social skills, spiritual and moral values for peaceful co-existence.
4. Explore, manipulate, manage and conserve the environment effectively for learning and sustainable development.
5. Practise relevant hygiene, sanitation and nutrition skills to promote health.
6. Demonstrate ethical behaviour and exhibit good citizenship as a civic responsibility.
7. Appreciate the country's rich and diverse cultural heritage for harmonious co-existence.
8. Manage pertinent and contemporary issues in society effectively.
9. Apply digital literacy skills for communication and learning.
ESSENCE STATEMENT
Agriculture and nutrition is a learning area that anchors on the United Nation Sustainable development goa ls and the socio-
economic pillar of Kenya Vision 2030 to promote health, hygiene, food and nutrition security through education. It is an
integrated learning area comprising of agriculture and home science  concepts introduced in the upper primary curriculu m. The
learners will deepen the acquired knowledge, skills, attitudes and values in conservation of resources, food production, hygiene
and innovative production techniques. The curriculum will enrich learner’s competencies in conservation of resources, crop and
animal production , foods and nutrition, personal and environmental hygiene , basic clothing construction and  laundry work.
Agriculture and nutrition curriculum will form grounds for specialization in respective career pathways in senior school and
beyond.
vi
GENERAL LEARNING OUTCOMES
By end of Junior School, the learner should be able to:
1. Participate actively in agricultural and household activities in conservation of resources.
2. Use scarce resources through innovative practices to contribute towards food and nutrition security.
3. Engage in food production processes for self-sustainability, health and economic development.
4. Adopt personal and environmental hygiene practices for healthy living.
5. Apply appropriate production techniques, innovative technologies,  digital and media resources to enhance sustainable
agricultural and household practices.
6. Appreciate agricultural and household skills as a worthy niche for hobby, career development, further education and
training.

APPENDIX 1: GUIDELINES FOR INTEGRATING COMMUNITY SERVICE LEARNING PROJECT
Introduction
In Grade 8, learners will undertake an integrated Community Service Learning (CSL) project of choice from a single or
combined subject. The CSL project will enable the learner to apply knowledge and skills from  other subjects to address a
problem in the community. The implementation of the integrated CSL project will take a Whole School Approach, where  all
members of the school community including teachers, school administration, parents/guardians/ local communi ty and support
staff. It will  be a collaborative effort where the teacher of Social Studies coordinates and works with other subject teachers to
design and implement the integrated CSL projects.   The teachers will select a theme drawn from different Learni ng Areas and
the broader categories of Pertinent and Contemporary Issues (PCIs) for the CSL project.  It should also provide an opportunity
for development of core competencies and  nurturing of values. Learners will undertake one common integrated class CSL
project following a 6-step milestone approach as follows:
Milestone Description
Milestone 1
Problem Identification
Learners study their community to understand the challenges faced and their effects on community members.
Some of the challenges in the community can be:
 Environmental degradation
 Lifestyle diseases, Communicable and non-communicable diseases
 Poverty
 Violence and conflicts in the community
 Food security issues
23
Milestone 2 Designing a solution
Learners create an intervention to address the challenge identified.
Milestone 3 Planning for the Project
Learners share roles, create a list of activities to be undertaken, mobilise resources needed to create their
intervention and set timelines for execution
Milestone 4 Implementation
The learners execute the project and keep evidence of work done.
Milestone 5 Showcasing /Exhibition and Report Writing
Exhibitions involve showcasing  learners’ project items to the community and reflecting on the feedback
Learners write a report detailing their project activities and learnings from feedback
Milestone 6 Reflection
Learners review all project work to learn from the challenges faced.
They link project work with academic concepts, noting how the concepts enabled them to do their
project as well as how the project helped to deepen learning of the academic concepts.
Note: The milestones will be staggered across the 3 terms of the academic calendar.
Assessment of CSL integrated Project
Assessment for the integrated  CSL project will be conducted formati vely. The assessment will consider both the process and
end product. This entails assessing each of the milestone stages of  the integrated CSL class project. It will focus on 3
components namely: skills from various learning areas applied in carrying out t he project, core competencies developed and
values nurtured.
24

NATIONAL GOALS OF EDUCATION
Education in Kenya should:
1. Foster nationalism and patriotism and promote national unity
Kenya’s people belong to different communities, races and religions, but these differences need not divide them. They must
be able to live and interact as Kenyans. It is a paramount duty of education to help young people acquire this sense of
nationhood by removing conflicts and promoting positive attitudes of mutual respect which enable them to live together in
harmony and foster patriotism in order to make a positive contribution to the life of the nation.
2. Promote the social, economic, technological and industrial needs for national development
Education should prepare the youth of the country to play an effective and productive role in the life of the nation.
i) Social Needs
Education in Kenya must prepare children for changes in attitudes and relationships which are necessary for the smooth
progress of a rapidly developing modern economy. There is bound to be a silent social revolution following in the wake of
rapid modernization. Education should assist our youth to adapt to this change.
ii) Economic Needs
Education in Kenya should produce citizens with the skills, knowledge, expertise and personal qualities that are required
to support a growing economy. Kenya is building up a modern and independent economy which is in need of an adequate
and relevant domestic workforce.
iii) Technological and Industrial Needs
Education in Kenya should provide learners with the necessary skills and attitudes for industrial development. Kenya
recognizes the rapid industrial and technological changes taking place, especially in the developed world. We can only be
part of this development if our education system is deliberately focused on the knowledge, skills and attitudes tha t will
prepare our young people for these changing global trends.
Page | iii
3. Promote individual development and self-fulfilment
Education should provide opportunities for the fullest development of individual talents and personality. It should help children
to develop their potential interests and abilities. A vital aspect of individual development is the building of character.
4. Promote sound moral and religious values
Education should provide for the development of knowledge, skills and attitudes that will enh ance the acquisition of
sound moral values and help children to grow up into self-disciplined, self-reliant and integrated citizens.
5. Promote social equity and responsibility
Education respect should promote social equality and foster a sense of social responsibility within an education system which
provides equal educational opportunities for all. It should give all children varied and challenging opportunities for collective
activities and corporate social service irrespective of gender, ability or geographical environment.
6. Promote for and development of Kenya’s rich and varied cultures
Education should instill in the youth of Kenya an understanding of past and present cultures and their valid place in
contemporary society. Children should be able to blend the best of traditional values with the changing requirements that must
follow rapid development in order to build a stable and modern society.
7. Promote international consciousness and foster positive attitudes towards other nations
Kenya is part of the international community. It is part of the complicated and interdependent network of peoples and nations.
Education should therefore lead the youth of the country to accept membership of t his international community with all the
obligations and responsibilities, rights and benefits that this membership entails.
Page | iv
8. Promote positive attitudes towards good health and environmental protection
Education should inculcate in young people the value of good health in order for them to avoid indulging in activities that will
lead to physical or mental ill health. It should foster positive attitudes towards environmental development and conservation .
It should lead the youth of Kenya to appreciate the need for a healthy environment.

LEARNING OUTCOMES FOR JUNIOR SCHOOL
By end of Junior School, the learner should be able to:
1. Apply literacy, numeracy and logical thinking skills for appropriate self-expression.
2. Communicate effectively, verbally and non-verbally, in diverse contexts.
3. Demonstrate social skills, spiritual and moral values for peaceful co-existence.
4. Explore, manipulate, manage and conserve the environment effectively for learning and sustainable development.
5. Practise relevant hygiene, sanitation and nutrition skills to promote health.
6. Demonstrate ethical behaviour and exhibit good citizenship as a civic responsibility.
7. Appreciate the country's rich and diverse cultural heritage for harmonious co-existence.
8. Manage pertinent and contemporary issues in society effectively.
9. Apply digital literacy skills for communication and learning.
Page | v
ESSENCE STATEMENT
We live in a world o Ma thematics whereby we count, add, subtract, multiply  or divide quantities and substances throughout our
daily interactions. Mathematics involves understanding numbers and the numerical operations used to develop strategies for mental
mathematical problem solving skills, estimation and computational fluency.  We live in a world of space, shape and structures. It
is impossible to think of a world without Mathematics. It is applied in the economic activities, scientific, social, religiou s and
political worlds. It is therefore imperative that children are taught Mathematics from early years.
In Junior Secondary, Mathematics builds on the competencies acquired by the learner from primary school. It enhances the learner's
competencies in mathematical skills as a foundation for Science, Technology, Engineering and M athematics (STEM) and other
pathways at Senior School. Mathematics also prepares the learner to have sufficient skills and competencies for application i n
solving problems in real life situations. This is in line with vision 2030 and sessional paper number  1 of 2019 which emphasizes
on STEM areas.
SUBJECT GENERAL LEARNING OUTCOMES
By the end of the Junior Secondary, the learner should be able to:
1) Demonstrate mastery of number concepts by working out problems in day to day life
2) Represent and apply algebraic expressions in different ways
3) Apply measurement skills to find solutions to problems in a variety of contexts
4) Use money and carry out financial transactions in real life situations
5) Generate geometrical shapes and describe spatial relationships in different contexts
6) Collect and organize data to inform and solve problems in real life situations
7) Develop logical thinking, reasoning, communication and application skills through a mathematical approach to problem
solving
8) Apply mathematical ideas and concepts to other learning areas or subjects and in real life contexts.
9) Develop confidence and interest in mathematics for further training and enjoyment.

COMMUNITY SERVICE LEARNING PROJECT
Introduction
In Grade 9, learners will undertake a CSL activity on thematic areas provided to them. They will be required to identify a
community problem through research, design solution and come up with a plan to solve the problem. The preparations will be
carried out in convenient groups. Learners will build on CSL knowledge, skills and attitudes acquired during Social Studies a s
well as other learning areas.
CSL Skills to be covered:
i) Leadership: Learners develop leadership skills as they undertake various roles during preparation.
ii) Financial Literacy and Entrepreneurship Skills: Learners will gain skills on wise spending, saving and investing for
sustained economic growth. They could consider ways of generating income as they undertake the CSL project through
innovative ways. Moreover, they could identify business ideas and opportunities as well as resources to meet the needs of the
community.
iii) Research: Learners will exploit research skills as they identify a problem or a pertinent issue in the community, design a
solution and plan how the problem will be solved. They will then do a report of the project accomplished.
iv) Communication and collaboration: Learners will develop these skills as they interrogate the problem in the society, research
and brainstorm on solution, and collaborate with the members of the community in the implementation process.
Page | 44
v) Citizenship: Learners will engage in the CSL activi ties, in appreciation of their responsibilities, rights and privileges as
citizens, giving them a sense of belonging and attachment to the nation. They will also be empowered to engage and assume
active roles in shaping a more cohesive, peaceful and inclusive society.
i) Life Skills: Learners will develop life skills in the areas of decision making, assertiveness, effective communication, and
problem solving and stress management.
ii) Community Development: Learners will be sensitized with the needs or gaps in the community, and empowered to take
responsibility within their means for stronger and more resilient communities.

NATIONAL GOALS OF EDUCATION
Education in Kenya should:
i) Foster nationalism and patriotism and promote national unity.
Kenya’s people belong to different communities, races and religions, but these differences need not divide them. They must be
able to live and interact as Kenyans. It is a paramount duty of education to help young people acquire this sense of nationho od
by removing conflicts and promoting positive attitudes of mutual respect which enable them to l ive together in harmony and
foster patriotism in order to make a positive contribution to the life of the nation.
ii) Promote the social, economic, technological and industrial needs for national development.
Education should prepare the youth of the country to play an effective and productive role in the life of the nation.
a) Social Needs
Education in Kenya must prepare children for changes in attitudes and relationships which are necessary for the
smooth progress of a rapidly developing modern economy. There  is bound to be a silent social revolution following
the wake of rapid modernisation. Education should assist our youth to adapt to this change.
b) Economic Needs
Education in Kenya should produce citizens with the skills, knowledge, expertise and personal q ualities that are
required to support a growing economy. Kenya is building up a modern and independent economy which is in need of
an adequate and relevant domestic workforce.
c) Technological and Industrial Needs
Education in Kenya should provide learners w ith the necessary skills and attitudes for industrial development. Kenya
recognises the rapid industrial and technological changes taking place, especially in the developed world. We can only
be part of this development if our education system is deliberat ely focused on the knowledge, skills and attitudes that
will prepare our young people for these changing global trends.
iii) Promote individual development and self-fulfilment
Education should provide opportunities for the fullest development of individual tal ents and personality. It should help
children to develop their potential interests and abilities. A vital aspect of individual development is the building of character.
iv) Promote sound moral and religious values.
Education should provide for the development  of knowledge, skills and attitudes that will enhance the acquisition of sound
moral values and help children to grow up into self-disciplined, self-reliant and integrated citizens.
v)  Promote social equality and responsibility.
Education should promote so cial equality and foster a sense of social responsibility within an education system which
provides equal educational opportunities for all. It should give all children varied and challenging opportunities for collec tive
activities and corporate social service irrespective of gender, ability or geographical environment.
vi) Promote respect for and development of Kenya’s rich and varied cultures.
Education should instil in the youth of Kenya an understanding of past and present cultures and their valid place i n
contemporary society. Children should be able to blend the best of traditional values with the changing requirements that mus t
follow rapid development in order to build a stable and modern society.
vii) Promote international consciousness and foster positive attitudes towards other nations.
Kenya is part of the international community. It is part of the complicated and interdependent network of peoples and nations .
Education should therefore lead the youth of the country to accept membership of this intern ational community with all the
obligations and responsibilities, rights and benefits that this membership entails.
viii.  Promote positive attitudes towards good health and environmental protection.
Education should inculcate in young people the value of good health in order for them to avoid indulging in activities that will
lead to physical or mental ill health. It should foster positive attitudes towards environmental development and conservation. It
should lead the youth of Kenya to appreciate the need for a healthy environment.

LEARNING OUTCOMES FOR JUNIOR SCHOOL
By end of Junior School, the learner should be able to:
1. Apply literacy, numeracy and logical thinking skills for appropriate self-expression.
2. Communicate effectively, verbally and non-verbally, in diverse contexts.
3. Demonstrate social skills, spiritual and moral values for peaceful co-existence.
4. Explore, manipulate, manage and conserve the environment effectively for learning and sustainable development.
5. Practise relevant hygiene, sanitation and nutrition skills to promote health.
6. Demonstrate ethical behaviour and exhibit good citizenship as a civic responsibility.
7. Appreciate the country's rich and diverse cultural heritage for harmonious co-existence.
8. Manage pertinent and contemporary issues in society effectively.
9. Apply digital literacy skills for communication and learning.
ESSENCE STATEMENT
The Constitution of Kenya , 2010 accords English the status of one of the official languages. According to the Lan guage in
Education Policy of 1976, English is the language of instruction from Grade Four onwards, including colleges and universities .
In addition, English is a language of communication at both local and international levels. Mastery of English enhances access to
academic, social, and professional opportunities. The English subject at the Junior Secondary School level will expose learne rs
to both knowledge and use of the English language, and literary appreciation. It will build on the competencies acquir ed at the
Upper Primary School level in Listening, Speaking, Reading, Writing, and Grammar in Use.
By the end of Junior Secondary School level, learners will be expected to gain proficiency in the English language for further
learning and training, and t heir day -to-day interactions. They will be provided with varied and appropriate experiences in
Listening, Speaking, Reading, Writing, and Grammar in Use to develop linguistic and communicative competence. They will
also be expected to interact with print and non-print language and literary material both in and outside the classroom.
The English subject will lay a firm foundation for the learners' efficient and effective use of the English language, as a
communication tool and the medium of instruction at S enior Secondary School level. In addition, it will be a stepping stone for
further study of English language, Literature in English and other pathways.
GENERAL LEARNING OUTCOMES FOR ENGLISH
By the end of Junior Secondary level, the learner should be able to:
1. Listen and respond appropriately to relevant information in a variety of contexts.
2. Read a wide variety of texts fluently, accurately, and interpretively for lifelong learning.
3. Develop critical thinking skills for life.
4. Read and analyse literary works and relate them to real life experiences.
5. Develop a lifelong interest in reading on a wide range of subjects.
6. Use grammatical forms to communicate appropriately in different settings.
7. Write texts legibly, creatively, and cohesively for life-long learning.
8. Apply digital literacy skills to enhance proficiency in English.
9. Appreciate the role of English as a medium for creativity and talent development.

Ways Of Reinforcing Cognitive Development
for JSS learners
Academic engagement
• Provide learning experiences that cater to their interest.
• Avoid negative labels such as “failure”. Focus on helping them progress
towards achievement of learning outcomes by providing constructive feedback
on tasks.
• Provide opportunities for learners to showcase competencies learnt and
compliment efforts. This enables them acquire self efficacy.
Reinforcing cognitive development cont’d
Build on already acquired knowledge, skills and values
• The learners will fall back on what they have learnt in previous grades as a
basis for understanding new content presented to them.
• Teachers should therefore link related knowledge and skills progressively
moving from known to unknown.
• Transfer of learning and reinforcement of learnt concepts will enhance
learning new knowledge and skills.
Reinforcing cognitive development cont’d
Provide Practical Learning Experiences
Engage learners in authentic learning experiences that connect to the world
around them. Provide experiential learning characterized by
• Learner-centered pedagogy,
• peer and self-assessment
• practical activities will be effective in promoting learning. A pragmatic
approach to instruction will enhance the achievement of learning outcomes.
Reinforcing cognitive development cont’d
Adopt instructional approaches that enable learners develop
competencies
▪ Involve the learner in discussions, experimentations, research and
debates over curricula, social, moral and global issues. This will
allow them to think critically.
▪ Provide learning experiences that allow for manipulation of
various ICT devices. Integration of ICT in learning will cater to the
interest of the learner thus making learning enjoyable.
Reinforcing cognitive development cont’d
Involve learners in decision making
• Learners can tell their strengths and weaknesses. Furthermore, they often
self-advocate. They are now able to identify areas they are good in and take
up tasks that they can competently execute.
• Learners should therefore be guided to set realistic goals for the future. Their
input is crucial in identifying skills and talents.
• Career guidance may also be given in line with the interests of the learner.
Physical Development at Puberty
Physiological
changes
- Acne
- Hormonal
imbalances Increase in
size and
weight
Breast
Development
Uterus and
ovarian
development
- Testicular
Development
- Wet dreams
Hips enlarge
- Voice
changes
- Growth of
pubic hair
Characteristics of Social and Emotional
Development among JSS learners
• Need to establish sexual identity
• Prone to bullying
• Seek independence from parents and have a growing need for
privacy.
• Take up new roles such as youth leaders in Church.
• Some exhibit low self-esteem due to the physical changes at
puberty.
• Are attracted to the opposite sex.
• Have emotional outbursts.
• Desire to fit in – Seek to have relevance in a peer group
Characteristics of Moral Development
among JSS learners
• They reason about do’s and don’t’s in term of what they consider
logical.
• Behaviour is easily influenced by peers.
• Attempt to justify wrong behaviour. Sometimes resorting to
pointing out the same behaviour in adults as justification.
“You smoke, why shouldn’t I?
• Are often rebellious and derive pleasure in breaking rules.
• Make comparison between rules and individual rights.
Ways Of Supporting the Physical, Moral, Social
and Emotional Development for JSS learners
• Teachers should posses morally, socially and emotionally sound
behaviour that learners can emulate.
• Provide learner support programmes in the school such as Peer
support groups and Guidance and counseling.
• Promote the Whole School Approach to development of values.
• Promote healthy interaction in school through a positive school
culture.
• Monitor the use of ICT devices especially access to internet sites.
• Strengthen pastoral programmes in school to support the moral
development of learners.

ii
NATIONAL GOALS OF EDUCATION
Education in Kenya should:
i) Foster nationalism and patriotism and promote national unity
The people of Kenya belong to different communities, races and religions, but these differences need not divide them. They
must be able to live and interact as Kenyans. It is a paramount duty of education to help young people ac quire this sense of
nationhood by removing conflicts and promoting positive attitudes of mutual respect, to live together in harmony and foster
patriotism, and to make a positive contribution to the life of the nation.
ii) Promote the social, economic, technological, and industrial needs for national development
Education should prepare the youth of the country to play an effective and productive role in the life of the nation.
a) Social Needs
Education in Kenya must prepare children for changes in attitudes and relationships, which are necessary for the smooth
progress of a rapidly developing modern economy. There is bound to be a silent social revolution following the wake of
rapid modernisation. Education should assist our youth to adapt to this change.
b) Economic Needs
Education in Kenya should produce citizens with the skills, knowledge, expertise, and personal qualities that are required to
support a growing economy. Kenya is building up a modern and independent economy that requires an adequate and relevant
domestic workforce.
c) Technological and Industrial Needs
Education in Kenya should provide learners with the necessary skills and attitudes for industrial development. Kenya
recognises the rapid industrial and technological changes taking place, especia lly in the developed world. We can only be
part of this development if our education system is deliberately focused on the knowledge, skills and attitudes that will
prepare our young people for these changing global trends.
iii) Promote individual development and self-fulfillment
Education should provide opportunities for the fullest development of individual talents and personality. It should help children
to develop their potential interests and abilities. A vital aspect of individual development is the building of character.
iii
iv) Promote sound moral and religious values
Education should provide for the development of knowledge, skills and attitudes that will enhance the acquisition of sound
moral values and help children to grow up into self-disciplined, self-reliant and integrated citizens.
v)  Promote social equality and responsibility
Education should promote social equality and foster a sense of social responsibility within an education system that provides
equal educational opportunities for all. It sh ould give all children varied and challenging opportunities for collective activities
and corporate social service irrespective of gender, ability or geographical environment.
vi) Promote respect for and development of Kenya’s rich and varied cultures
Education should instill in the youth of Kenya an understanding of past and present cultures and their valid place in contemporary
society. Children should be able to blend the best of traditional values with the changing requirements that must follow rapi d
development to build a stable and modern society.
vii) Promote international consciousness and foster positive attitudes towards other nations
Kenya is part of the international community. It is part of the complicated and interdependent network of peoples and n ations.
Education should therefore lead the youth of the country to accept membership of this international community with all the
obligations and responsibilities, rights and benefits that this membership entails.
viii.  Promote positive attitudes towards good health and environmental protection
Education should inculcate in young people the value of good health for them to avoid indulging in activities that will lead to
physical or mental ill health. It should foster positive attitudes towards environmental development and conservation. It should
lead the youth of Kenya to appreciate the need for a healthy environment.
iv

(40 minutes per lesson)

LEVEL LEARNING OUTCOMES FOR MIDDLE SCHOOL
By the end of Middle School, the learner should be able to:
1. Apply literacy, numeracy and logical thinking skills for appropriate self-expression.
2. Communicate effectively, verbally and non-verbally, in diverse contexts.
3. Demonstrate social skills, spiritual and moral values for peaceful co-existence.
4. Explore, manipulate, manage, and conserve the environment effectively for learning and sustainable development.
5. Practise relevant hygiene, sanitation and nutrition skills to promote health.
6. Demonstrate ethical behaviour and exhibit good citizenship as a civic responsibility.
7. Appreciate the country's rich and diverse cultural heritage for harmonious coexistence.
8. Manage pertinent and contemporary issues in society effectively.
9. Apply digital literacy skills for communication and learning.
ESSENCE STATEMENT
Christians Religious Education is the study of God’s self -revelation to man through creation, the Bible, the life and Ministry of
Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit.  The curriculum is spiral hence, concepts at this grade build on concepts and skills learnt in Grade
7 and 8. Christian Religious Education facilitates the learner to acquire basic principles of Christian living, which enable them to
develop spiritually, morally, emotionally, and intellectually . The learner is  therefore, exposed to a broad range of biblical
experiences for character formation and upright living. The five strands are deliberate in developing the intellectual skills necessary
for moral living including reflection, discernment, critical thinking, and deciding how to  act in accordance with an informed
conscience.
The method of teaching and learning CRE is Life Approach. This is in line with the constructivist theory and socio-cultural theory
that aims at enabling the learner to construct knowle dge through varied experiences. The learner will  therefore, use Christian
insights to critically analyse, evaluate and judge the issues he/she is facing in life. The competencies acquired at this level equips
the learner with knowledge, skills, values and attitudes required as they transition to senior School.
vi
SUBJECT GENERAL LEARNING OUTCOMES
By the end of Junior School, the learner should be able to:
1. Demonstrate an awareness of the love of God as the Sole Creator and Heavenly Father by being good stewards of His creation.
2. Analyse teachings in the Holy Bible for moral, spiritual and character development, and growth.
3. Apply the teachings of Jesus Christ in their day-to-day lives to promote social equality and responsibility.
4. Appreciate the role of the church in promoting spiritual transformation and good citizenship.
5. Evaluate contemporary, social and moral issues, which affect the society and equip him/her with knowledge and skills to make
informed decisions.
6. Utilise knowledge and skills of Information Communication and Technology in the learning of Christian Religious Education

COMMUNITY SERVICE LEARNING PROJECT
Introduction
In Grade 9, learners will undertake a CSL activity on t hematic areas provided to them. They will be required to identify  a
community problem through research, design a solution and come up with a plan to solve the problem. The preparations will be
carried out in convenient groups. Learners will build on CSL knowledge, skills and attitudes acquired during Social Studies as
well as other learning areas.
CSL Skills to be covered:
i) Leadership: Learners develop leadership skills as they undertake various roles during preparation.
ii) Financial Literacy and Entrepreneurship Skills: Learners will gain skills in wise spending, saving and investing for
sustained economic growth. They could consider ways of generating income as they undertake the CSL  project through
innovative ways. Moreover, they could identify business ideas and opportunities, as well as resources to meet the needs of
the community.
iii) Research: Learners will exploit research skills as they identify a problem or a pertinent issue in the community, design a
solution and plan how the problem will be solved. They will then prepare a report of the project accomplished.
iv) Communication and collaboration:  Learners will develop these skills as they interrogate the problem in the society,
research and brainstorm on a solution and collaborate with members of the community in the implementation process.
v) Citizenship: Learners will engage in the CSL activities, in appreciation of their responsibilities, rights and privileges as
citizens, giving them a sense of belonging and attachment to the nation. They will also be empowered to engage and assume
active roles in shaping a more cohesive, peaceful and inclusive society.
vi) Life Skills: Learners will develop life skills in the areas of decision-making, assertiveness, effective communication,
problem-solving, and stress management.
vii) Community Development: Learners will be sensitized with the needs or gaps in the community, and empowered to take
responsibility within their means for stronger and more resilient communities.

INTRODUCTION
• French language is one of the foreign languages taught in Kenyan schools. In
the competency-based curriculum, the French language is taught from grade
4. At grade 7, learners cover the four skills, listening and speaking, reading
and writing. These four skills are further broken down to sub skills. In Strand
three, the writing skill is broken down into; guided writing, descriptive
writing, creative writing and functional creative writing.
Essence statement:
French at Junior secondary builds on the linguistic competencies acquired in
upper primary. The proposed learning experiences provide the opportunity
to experiment with and explore the language in contextualized
communication situations. The content is delivered using interactive and
participatory methods of learning aimed at unlocking the learners ‘multiple
intelligences.

Unique Area
Intercultural approach
• Learning French as a foreign language calls for an appreciation of the French culture on which the language
itself is anchored. In this case, the Intercultural learning approach involves exposing the learners to various
aspects of the way of life in the francophone world before requiring them to compare these with what goes
on in their own cultures.
• Learners are exposed to virtual visits to sites of interest in the francophone world to enrich their
experiences.
• Learners could use language learning applications on the internet and create communities of learning to
develop their intercultural awareness skills. Such practice will help in developing positive attitude and a
good measure of tolerance of other cultures. These approach enables the learners to observe, to compare,
and to contrast their culture and the French culture, thereby raising their awareness and understanding
these will make them accept and appreciate cultural differences. For instance,in sub strand 1.7Listening
Comprehension and Oral expression: Hobbies, you could engage the learners in learning activities where
they compare hobby activities in Kenya and France.
Approche actionnelle
• In this approach, the learner is considered a social actor
in the learning process- an active participant who engages
in tasks in a cultural contextor real life experience.
• The learner is given a realistic scenario with a problem to
solve. an inclusive and social environment is cultivated to
promote cooperation.
• Discussion in pairs or groups are encouraged to create a
sense of belonging in the community.

1.0 INTRODUCTION
The Kenya Institute of Curriculum Development (KICD) has developed curriculum designs
for Grade 7, 8 and 9 for learners following age based pathway and Prevocational  Level for
learners following stage based pathway. To ensure effective delivery of the cur riculum, the
Institute in collaboration with the Teachers Service Commission (TSC) has organised
elaborate training programmes for teachers in Junior School and Prevocational Level.
KICD has developed this Facilitators Training Manual to enable training of curriculum
implementers for efficient curriculum implementation in Grade 7, 8 and 9 and Prevocational
Level. The training manual focuses on the pedagogical approaches of facilitating learning to
different categories of learners with special needs. Further, the manual guides participants on
how to adapt resources and assessment methods in the various subjects/learning areas in
junior school and pre vocational level.
Aims of the Training
The aims of the training are to:
a) equip participants with the necessary knowledge, skills and attitudes to effectively
implement the Competency Based Curriculum;
b) equip participants with skills to facilitate differentiated inclusive learning to ensure
that all learners are fully engaged in the learning process.
Structure of the Manual
In each session, the manual outlines the following:
• Session outcomes.
• Session activity.
• Facilitators notes.
• Reflections.
SESSION 1: INTRODUCTION
This session addresses the overview of Junior school for learners with visual, hearing,
physical impairment as well as learners in pre vocational level of the stage based pathway.
Note : Graduate from primary school joins junior school at grade 7.
By the end of the session, the participant should be able to
a) describe characteristics of learners in junior school and pre-vocational level.
b) examine learner centres pedagogies for junior school and pre vocational level
In groups, participants
a) brainstorm on the overview of junior school and pre-vocational level and do a plenary
presentation
b) discuss on the characteristics of learners in junior school and at pre vocational level

Facilitator’s notes
Learners join the junior school after completing upper primary.  Junior School exposes learners
to a broad based curriculum to enable them to explore their own abilities, personality and
potential as a basis for choosing subjects according to career paths of interest at the senior
school. Learners in junior school are exposed to all  learning areas to enable them make
informed choices as they transition to senior school. Learners learn in junior school for a
duration of three years.

LEARNER CENTRED PEDAGOGIES FOR JUNIOR SCHOOL
Pedagogy refers to sets of learning experiences that facilitate achievement of specified learning
outcomes. Learner centered pedagogical approaches include:
Inquiry Based learning:
• Learners construct knowledge and meaning from their own experiences.
• Learners are engaged in, questioning, reasoning and experiential (hands-on activities).
Problem-based learning (PBL)
• Learners are involved in solving authentic, open-ended, structured, real-world problems.
• Learners are engaged in extended processes of asking questions, finding resources and
applying learnt information.
Play Based Learning
• Employs plays as the primary means for learners to explore the world, investigate its properties
and build an understanding of how it works.
• Play fosters curiosity, creativity, and problem-solving skills. It supports learners’ well-being,
resilience, motivation and engagement & prepares learners for life- long learning.
Project Based Learning
• Learners gain knowledge and skills by working for an extended period of time to investigate
and respond to authentic, engaging and complex tasks, questions, problems or challenges.
• Learners drive their own learning through inquiry, as they work collaboratively to research and
create projects that reflect their innate potential and talents.
Blended Learning
Involves integrating traditional face-to-face instruction with technology.
Cooperative learning
Involves learners working in small groups collaboratively to accomplish assigned tasks.
Design-based learning (DBL)
Entails the use of open ended, hands -on and challenging experiences that allow learners to apply
theoretical knowledge to develop new ways of solving real-life problems.
Experiential learning
This is learning through reflection, where Learning Experiences are structured and learners take
initiative, make decisions and are accountable for the results. Examples include field trips and
excursions.
OVERVIEW OF PREVOCATIONAL LEVEL
PREVOCATIONAL LEVEL CURRICULUM
The specialised curriculum at the prevocational level, which is predominantly skill- based,
prepares learners with disabilities for basic work skills. At this level, learners are introduced to the
pre-requisite skills in various vocational skill areas to enable them to identify their abilities and
interests in a given field.
The Prevocational Level curriculum designs have been developed for the following categories of
learners with special needs; learners with Intellectual Disability, Deafblindness, Severe Autism,
Severe Cerebral Palsy and Multiple Disabilities.
Categories of Learners at Prevocational Level
Learners with Intellectual disabilities
These are learners with significant subaverage general intellectual functioning existing concurrently
with deficits in adaptive behaviour and manifested during the developmental period that adversely
affects the learner’s educational performance. Learners with intellectual disabilities are classified
into four major categories. These are learners with:
• Mild Intellectual Disabilities
• Moderate Intellectual Disabilities
• Severe Intellectual Disabilities
• Profound Intellectual Disabilities
Characteristics of learners with intellectual disabilities
● Slowness in learning due to delayed rate of intellectual development.
● Being unnecessarily slow in carrying out tasks.
● Learning and memory capabilities are significantly below average in comparison to peers
without disabilities.
● Are deficient in relating information to new situations
● Not able to understand what is said or follow instructions.
● Having trouble focusing on relevant stimuli in learning and in real life situations.
● Having difficulty in both learning and applying skills for a number of reasons, including a
higher level of distractibility, inattentiveness, failure to read social cues, and impulsive
behaviour.
● Having delayed speech, language comprehension and formulation difficulties.
● Failing to develop social and emotional relationships
● Having retarded motor development.
● Lacking rhythm in movement
● Having difficulties in remembering experiences or things learnt.
● Lacking motivation.
● Excessive drooling
● Having excessive purposeless movements
● Having difficulty in paying attention or focusing on an activity to its completion.
● Having difficulty in seeing the consequences of their actions.
● Have slow cognitive processing time.
● Have limited self-care skills and independent living skills
Learners with Deafblindness
These are learners with concomitant visual and hearing impairments, the combination of which
causes such severe communication and other developmental and education needs.
Categories of Learners who are deafblind
Learners with deafblindness are of four categories:
• Congenitally deafblind.
• Congenitally deaf with acquired blindness
• Congenitally blind with acquired deafness.
• Adventitiously deafblind (Aquired Deafness and Aquired Blindness).
General Characteristics of learners who are deafblind
● Difficulty communicating or an inability to communicate in a meaningful way.
● Have a distorted perception of the world.
● Have difficulty in establishing and maintaining interpersonal relationships information from
the surrounding.
● Have medical problems that lead to serious developmental delays.
● Presence of a combined vision and hearing losses
10
● Tactile sensitivity and resistance to being touched.
● Delays in motor development.
● Difficulty following a conversation
● Appear to be withdrawn and isolated
● May be deprived of many of the most basic extrinsic motivations
● Self-stimulatory behaviours resulting from sensory deprivation, isolation, frustration,
confusion and fear.
● Have unique learning styles.
● Difficulty in generalizing information learned to other settings.
● Feeding difficulties and or unusual sleeping patterns.
● May have difficulty anticipating what is going to happen. Clues from the environment or from
the faces/actions of others may be difficult to read.
● Difficulty navigating the environment
Learners with Autism spectrum disorders (ASDs)
Autism spectrum disorders are neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by an impairment in
social reciprocity, atypical communication, and repetitive behaviours. Learners with ASDs often
have difficulties with social communication and interaction, and restricted or repetitive behaviors
or interests. Further, they may also have different ways of learning, moving, or paying attention.
Characteristics of learners with Autism spectrum disorders
● Lines up toys or other objects and gets upset when order is changed.
● Repeats words or phrases over and over (echolalia).
● Plays with toys the same way every time.
● Is focused on parts of objects (for example, wheels).
● Gets upset by minor changes.
● Has obsessive interests.
● Tendency toward following certain routines routine.
● Difficult time with social interactions.
● Stereotyped movements such as flaps hands, rocks body, or runs/spins self in circles, flipping
light switches, hand waving, toe walking.
● Has unusual reactions to the way things sound, smell, taste, look, or feel.
● Delayed language skills.
● Delayed movement skills.
● Delayed cognitive or learning skills.
● Hyperactive, impulsive, and/or inattentive behaviour.
● Has epilepsy or seizure disorder.
● Unusual eating and sleeping habits.
● Gastrointestinal issues (for example, constipation)
● Unusual mood or emotional reactions.
11
● Anxiety, stress, or excessive worry.
● Lack of fear or more fear than expected.
Learners with Severe Cerebral palsy (CP)
Cerebral palsy is a disorder of movement and posture that is caused by a nonprogressive
abnormality of the immature brain that affect the learner’s ability to move and maintain balance
and posture. Learners with Cerebral Palsy are classified into four major categories. These are
learners with;
• increased muscle tone/ stiff muscles (Spastic Cerebral Palsy)
• abnormalities in muscle tone that involve the whole body/ uncontrollable movements
(Dyskinetic Cerebral Palsy.)
• abnormalities of voluntary movement involving balance and position of the trunk and
limbs in space/ poor balance and coordination (Ataxic Cerebral Palsy.)
• more than one type of cerebral palsy/ more than one type of motor pattern is present
(Mixed Cerebral Palsy.)
General characteristics of learners with severe cerebral palsy
● Stiff muscles and exaggerated reflexes (spasticity)
● Variations in muscle tone, such as being either too stiff or too floppy
● Stiff muscles with normal reflexes (rigidity)
Lack of balance and muscle coordination (ataxia)
● Tremors or jerky involuntary movement
● Slow, writhing movements
● Difficulty walking
● Difficulty with fine motor skills
● Difficulty speaking
● Excessive drooling or problems with swallowing
● Intellectual disabilities
● Delayed growth, resulting in smaller size than would be expected
● Presence of Seizures (epilepsy)
● Difficulty hearing (deafness)
● Problems with vision and abnormal eye movements
● Abnormal touch or pain sensations
● Bladder and bowel problems, including constipation and urinary incontinence
Learners with Multiple disabilities.
These are learners who have a combination of disabilities. For example, some learners have a
sensory disability with autism, intellectual and/or physical disabilities.
12
General characteristics of learners with multiple disabilities
● Appear to be withdrawn and isolated
● Have difficulty in establishing and maintaining interpersonal relationships
● Have limited self-care skills and independent living skills
● Have medical problems that leads to serious developmental delays.
● Are defensive of being touched.
● Have feeding difficulties and or unusual sleeping patterns.
● May display an immature behavior inconsistent with chronological age.
● May exhibit an impulsive behavior and low frustration level.
● May execute self-injurious behavior.
● Limited speech or communication.
● Difficulty in basic physical mobility.
● Trouble generalizing skills from one situation to another.
● Need for support in major life activities.

LEARNER CENTRED PEDAGOGIES FOR PREVOCATIONAL LEVEL
Pedagogy refers to sets of learning experiences that facilitate achievement of specific learning
outcomes. Some of the learner centred pedagogical approaches for Prevocational level include:
a)     Task Analysis
● Involves breaking down of concepts into smaller, manageable steps to make learning
more achievable.
b)    Diagnostic Prescriptive Instruction approach
● Emphasises assessing (diagnosing) the learners' individual learning needs and
providing adapted instruction (prescribing) to address those specific needs.
● This approach is highly learner-centred and focuses on understanding learners'
strengths and weaknesses to create targeted interventions for improvement.
c)     Multisensory Approach
13
● This involves incorporating visual, auditory, tactile and kinesthetic elements into the
instruction during learning. It also employs use of gestures, facial expressions, and
tactile cues to convey meaning and pairing spoken language with corresponding signs
or tactile representations to reinforce comprehension.
d)    Differentiated learning
● This is an instructional approach that tailors learning strategies, content, and
assessments to accommodate the diverse needs, skills, interests, and learning styles of
learners. Its goal is to ensure that all learners, regardless of their abilities or
backgrounds, have access to the same educational opportunities and can achieve their
highest potential. Differentiation can be applied in various areas of instruction,
including content, process, product, and learning environment.
e)     Modelling
● Modelling is a teaching strategy where the teacher demonstrates a task, skill, or concept
for the learners to observe and imitate. It involves the teacher showing how to perform
a task or solve a problem step-by-step while providing clear, direct examples of the
desired behaviors, tasks, or learning outcomes for learners to observe and imitate.
f)      Tactile Communication and feedback
● Involves using tactile Sign Language, hand-under- hand guidance, or tactile cues
depending on the individual needs of the learner.
● Learners are provided with meaningful touch cues to convey information and reinforce
learning.
g)     Routines
● Involves creating a structured, predictable sequences of activities or behaviours that are
consistently followed in the learning environment and communicating changes on time.
● Routines are integral to creating a structured and safe classroom atmosphere and helps
learners to anticipate what comes next and engage more fully.
● Routines provide stability and a sense of security, which can significantly reduce
anxiety and improve focus.
h)    Repetition
● This refers to the practice of repeatedly presenting information, instructions, tasks, or
activities to help learners gain mastery over them. It provides learners with additional
opportunities to practice and reinforce concepts until they are understood and can be
performed independently.
i)   Picture Exchange Communication System (PECS)
● This is an augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) approach used to
support learners with communication difficulties, particularly those with autism
spectrum disorder (ASD) and other developmental disabilities. PECS utilises pictures
or symbols to help students express their wants, needs, and ideas when verbal
communication is limited or absent. PECS empowers learners to communicate more
effectively, increasing their social interaction, independence, and overall quality of life.
j)      Inquiry Based Learning
● Learners construct knowledge and meaning from their own experiences.
14
● Learners are engaged in questioning, reasoning and experiential (hands-on activities)
k)    Problem-Based Learning (PBL)
● Learners are involved in solving authentic, open-ended, structured, real-world
problems.
● Learners are engaged in extended processes of asking questions, finding resources and
applying learnt information.
l)      Play Based Learning
● Employs play as the primary means for learners to explore the world, investigate its
properties and build an understanding of how it works.
● Play fosters curiosity, creativity, and problem-solving skills. It supports learners’ well-
being, resilience, motivation and engagement and prepares learners for life-long
learning.
● Play improves coordination, motor and social skills.
m)   Project Based Learning
● Learners gain knowledge and skills by working for an extended period of time to
investigate and respond to authentic, engaging and complex tasks, questions, problems
or challenges.
● Learners drive their own learning through inquiry, as they work collaboratively to
research and create projects that reflect their innate potential and talents.
n)    Blended Learning
● Involves integrating traditional face-to-face instruction with technology.
● Encourages incorporating use of assistive technology tools and software that can
support  the different categories learners  in their learning
o)     Design-Based Learning (DBL)
● Entails the use of open-ended, hands-on and challenging experiences that allow
learners to apply theoretical knowledge to develop new ways of solving real-life
problems.
● It encourages active learning through pursuing individual learner’s interests, providing
a real-world context to learning, while providing intrinsic motivation.
p)    Cooperative learning
● Involves learners working in small groups collaboratively to accomplish assigned tasks.
q)    Experiential Learning
● This is learning through active engagement with materials. Experiential learning helps
learners to gain practical skills, develop critical thinking skills, problem-solving
abilities and positive attitudes and help to enhance their communication and
collaboration skills. This type of learning can take many forms, including hands-on
activities, simulations, group projects, field trips, apprenticeships that allow learners to
apply theoretical knowledge to real-world experiences.

SESSION 2: INTERPRETATION OF CURRICULUM DESIGNS
Introduction
This session guides participants to identify and interpret the components of the curriculum design
for effective implementation of CBC.
By the end of the session, the participant should be able to:
a) Identify the components of the curriculum designs for effective implementation.
b) Interpret the curriculum designs for effective implementation of learning.
a) Participants peruse through extracts of curriculum designs to identify the components of
curriculum designs.
b) Participants discuss the various components of curriculum designs with emphasis on how
they are interrelated and developed and make presentations in plenary.
Facilitators Notes
Components and interpretation of the curriculum design
The following are the components of a curriculum design and how they are interpreted in CBC.
● National Goals of Education
● Level learning outcomes
● Essence statement
● Subject general learning outcomes
● Strands and sub strands
● Specific learning outcomes
● Suggested learning experiences
● Suggested Key Inquiry Question(s)
● Core competences
● Pertinent and Contemporary Issues
● Values
● Link to other subjects
● Suggested Non-formal activity to support learning
● Suggested learning resources
● Suggested assessment methods
● Suggested assessment rubric
● Community Service Learning
16
National goals of education
These are the goals that the country has set to achieve through provision of accessible, quality and
relevant education. Kenya has eight national goals that should be achieved through education.
Level learning outcomes
These are demonstrable attributes that are expected in a learner after completing a given level of
education, for example middle school education or Prevocational level.
Essence Statement
An essence statement gives a general overview of a subject. It summarises the fundamental ideas of
each subject. It also explains the rationale and justification of inclusion of the subjects in the
curriculum
Strand and Sub Strand
● A strand is a broad area of study within a specific subject. It is a consistent phenomenological
idea or concept that runs through the subject.
● A strand also cuts across all levels of education.
● A sub-strand represents smaller concepts within the strand.
Learning outcomes
They are the end result of what the learner is able to demonstrate upon completion of a lesson, sub -
strand, strand, subject or level.
Categories of learning outcomes
i) Level learning outcomes
These are the demonstrable end results expected in learners after having gone through a specific
level of CBC education. For example, Early Years, Middle School Education and Senior School
Education. They are stated in general terms.
ii) General learning outcomes
These learning outcomes indicate what the learner is expected to achieve in a given subject
iii) Specific Learning Outcomes
Specific learning outcomes indicate the expected observable changes in the learner after covering
a sub -strand or a lesson. They specify what the learner should know, is able to do and
demonstrate after participating and completing a given sub-strand or lesson.
• Outcomes are usually expressed through the application of knowledge, skills and attitudes.
Specific learning outcome should have the following components:
• The action verb (the verb represents the three domains of learning including knowledge,
skills and attitudes).
• The object of the verb (the outcome should also have an object, which answers the question
“what”).
• The context (the outcome also has a context, which answers the questions “why”, “where”,
‘’how” and “when”).
17
Suggested learning experiences
Learning experiences comprise of activities that the learner is engaged in during the lesson. The
activities may be carried out by an individual learner or as a group work activity. However, they
should ultimately enable the learner to achieve the intended specific learning outcomes of the lesson.
Learning experiences enable the learner to:
• Acquire knowledge, skills and develop attitudes
• Acquire the intended competences
• Acquire values, pertinent and contemporary issues
• Learn from one another
• Self-regulate and evaluate
• Engage deeply in the subject matter
• Reflect on the learning process
• Interact with others during the learning process
Key Inquiry Question(s)
Key Inquiry Question(s) (KIQ) is an approach where the teacher uses questions to prod learners
thinking to allow them to create information using their own words and understanding. They;
• help to focus the learning,
• probe for deeper meaning and set the stage for further questioning,
• foster the development of critical thinking skills and higher order capabilities such as
problem solving,
• allow learners to explore ideas in an open-ended, non-judgmental, meaningful and
purposeful way,
• encourage collaboration amongst learners, teachers, and the community and integrate
technology to support the learning process.
Writing Key Inquiry Question(s)
Consider the focus of your learning outcome and the sub strands as given in the curriculum design
Core Competencies to be developed
A competency is the ability to apply appropriate knowledge, skills, attitudes and values to
successfully perform a task. Core Competencies are sets of intellectual, personal, social and
emotional proficiencies that students should develop in order to engag e in deep, lifelong
learning. The core competencies are developed through exposing the learner to stimulating
learning experiences. The learning areas serve as vehicles through which the core competencies
are developed over time.
The seven core competencies to be developed are:
• Communication and collaboration
• Critical thinking and problem solving
• Imagination and creativity
• Digital literacy
• Citizenship
• Learning to learn and
• Self-efficacy.
18
VALUES
These are principles, qualities ,  beliefs or standards that guide an individual  to respond or
behave in a given circumstance or situation.Values influence how we feel, act and make
choices in life. Nurturing of values will facilitate the achievement of moulding ethical citizens.
Values are intended to address the prevailing societal challenges and usher in a desirable future.
The eight core values which have been mainstreamed in CBC are:
▪ Love
▪ Responsibility
▪ Respect
▪ Unity
▪ Peace
▪ Patriotism
▪ Social Justice
▪ Integrity
Values  should be mainstreamed through the whole  school approach. Mainstreaming is the
process of identifying suitable opportunities in specific learning areas, where values can be
incorporated in the learning experiences.
PERTINENT AND CONTEMPORARY ISSUES (PCIS)
PCIs are salient issues that have the potential to affect learner’s psychosocial wellbeing,
access to education, retention, transition, completion and ultimately advancement in the
world of work. Education is supposed to equip learners with cognitive and psychosocial
competencies and values necessary in addressing challenges of everyday life.
The PCIs mainstreamed in the learning areas are in four categories:
1. Citizenship: Peace education, Integrity, Ethnic and racial relations, Social cohesion,
Patriotism and Good governance, Child’s rights, Child care and protection.
2. Health Promotion: HIV and AIDS, Alcohol and Substance use, Life style diseases,
personal hygiene, Prevention of Communicable and non communicable diseases,
Menstrual Disorders prevention among others.
3. Life Skills Education, Moral Education and human sexuality Education.
4. Social –economic Issues: Environmental Education, Disaster Risk Reduction ,Safety &
security, radicalization & terrorism prevention education, child care & protection, Gender
and Animal Welfare Education and indigenous knowledge.
19
Link to other subjects/ learning areas
This refers to the relationship between two or more subjects/learning areas. It is a conscious
effort to use learning of concepts in one subject/learning area to relate to learning of concepts
in another subjects/learning area. This requires integration of  learning to enable the learner to
make connections across strands and sub strands of different subjects/learning areas. The
teacher should also use related concepts in other subjects/learning areas to reinforce concepts
in the given subjects/learning area. The awareness of linkages between subjects/learning areas
gives an opportunity to borrow and share learning resources in different subjects/learning areas,
thus optimising on available resources.
Suggested Learning Resources
These are any materials, tools and persons that teachers and learners use to facilitate learning
and understanding of concepts. Learning resources make learning real, practical and
pleasurable for the learners.
Suggested Assessment methods
Assessment methods are the strategies and procedures of collecting information to determine
the extent to which learners demonstrate achievement of the specified learning outcomes.
The main purpose of assessing learners is to:
● Inform learning decisions
● Establish the level of learner’s competence
● Ascertain progress against the learning outcomes
● Encourage learners to make judgments about their performance
● Enhance learner motivation
● Identify where intervention, focused support or referral is required
● Make decisions regarding choice of subject, course and careers pathways.
Some of the assessment method include:
● Written assignment
● Observation,
● Oral questioning
● Peer assessment
● Self-assessment
● Project work
Assessment rubric

SPECIFIC LEARNING OUTCOME:
By the end of the sub strand, the learner should be able to;
a) Identify the place value and total value of digits in decimals in real life.
LESSON LEARNING OUTCOMES:
By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to;
a) identify the place value of digits in decimal numbers,
b) work out the place value of digits in decimal numbers using place value charts,
c) desire to use decimals in real life situations.
LEARNING EXPERIENCES:
Guide learners individually, in purposive pairs or groups to:
• Observe and discuss virtual or actual samples to locate the place values of specific digits in a decimal
number from the place value chart. Learners with manipulation difficulties could be assisted by peers or
use assistive technology to perform the task. Learners with speech difficulties could use Augmentative
and Alternative modes of Communication. Communication and collaboration will be developed as the
learners work in pairs or groups to identify the place value and total value of decimal numbers. Inquiry
based learning may be used as learners observe and discuss virtual or actual samples to locate the
place values of specific digits in a decimal number from the place value chart.
• Work out the place value of digits in decimal numbers using place value apparatus and worksheets.
Problem based learning as learners work out the place value of digits in decimal numbers using place
value apparatus and worksheets. Unity is enhanced as the learner cooperates and works harmoniously
with peers to find the place value of digits in decimal numbers.
• Use adapted ICT devices to learn more about place value of digits in decimals. Learners with lower
extremities could be provided with footboards for tablets/ keyboards. Adjust light/ glare on the screens
of the digital devices appropriately for learners who are sensitive to light. Digital literacy is enhanced as
learners use digital devices in searching. Responsibility and integrity is nurtured as they operate the
digital devices.  Cooperative learning could be used during group activities as learners use ICT devices
to learn more about place value of digits in decimals.
ASSESSMENT METHODS:
• Observation - during observation the teacher should consider learners functional ability.
• Oral questions - learners with speech difficulties could use alternative modes of communication to
respond. They could also be given more time to respond.
• Written test -learners with manipulation difficulties could use adapted writing tools or assistive devices
to type their response. They could also answer the questions orally as they are recorded or be supported
by a scribe to write their responses. In addition, they could be given additional time.
LEARNING RESOURCES
Place value charts of appropriate size to enable easy manipulation, Number cards of appropriate size,
worksheets, Abacus, course book, adapted digital devices, adapted writing tools such heavy gauge paper,
universal cuffs, book holders

a)      outline process of diffusion and osmosis in cells
Lesson learning outcomes:
By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to;
a)  explain diffusion in a cell,
b)  illustrate the process of diffusion in a cell,
c)  appreciate the process of diffusion in living organisms.
LEARNING EXPERIENCES
● In groups, learners search for meaning of diffusion in a cell. Learners with blindness use
digital devices with screen readers or braille books while learners with low vision use digital
devices with screen magnifiers and contrasting background or print materials in appropriate
font and colour contrast. The competency of Digital literacy is developed as learners use
digital devices to search for information on the meaning of diffusion in a cell.  The PCI of
safety and security is enhanced as learners observ e safety while searching for information
from the internet. Blended learning is applied as learners utilize digital devices, print and
braille materials in searching for information on the meaning of diffusion.
● Learners with low vision watch videos and animation, observe pictures and charts showing
the process of diffusion. Learners with blindness listen to audio visual clips and animations
on the process of diffusion. The value of responsibility is enhanced as l earners take care of
the learning resources.
● Learners with low vision make a representation showing movement of particles during
diffusion using locally available materials. Learners clear their working areas after making
their representations. Learners with blindness give the description of the process of diffusion.
The PCI of Environmental conservation is achieved as learners use locally available
materials to make tactile diagrams. The value of responsibility is nurtured as learners clean
their working areas. The competency of creativity and imagination is developed as learners
use locally available materials to illustrate the process of diffusion.
Adaptation of Assessment
● Presentation of the task: A task should be presented in accessible format for learners with low
vision and blindness. Written test should be presented in appropriate font and colour contrast for
learners with low vision while in braille for learners with blindness.
44
● Collaborative assessment: Learners with blindness should be paired with sighted peers during
assessment on activities that require sight for example when watching video clips, observing pictures
and charts on process of diffusion.
● Time: Adequate time should be allocated during the assessment to allow learners undertake the
assessment.
● Response: Learners should be allowed to respond to assessment in the most suitable way. For
example, learners who challenges with writing and reading be provided with scribes.
● Assessment tools: Appropriate assessment tools should be utilized depending on the assessment
task. For example, a rubric can be used in assessment this lesson.
Learning Resources
● Digital devices with assistive technology such as screen readers, screen magnifiers, adapted
keyboard.
● Charts and pictures in appropriate font and colour contrast.
● Videos and animations with contrasting background, audio visual clips and animations with clear
audio verbal descriptions
● Print and Braille course books
● Locally available materials such as sand, glue and cartons
