LEARNER CENTRED PEDAGOGIES FOR JUNIOR SCHOOL
Pedagogy refers to sets of learning experiences that facilitate achievement of specified learning
outcomes. Learner centered pedagogical approaches include:
Inquiry Based learning:
• Learners construct knowledge and meaning from their own experiences.
• Learners are engaged in, questioning, reasoning and experiential (hands-on activities).
Problem-based learning (PBL)
• Learners are involved in solving authentic, open-ended, structured, real-world problems.
• Learners are engaged in extended processes of asking questions, finding resources and
applying learnt information.
Play Based Learning
• Employs plays as the primary means for learners to explore the world, investigate its properties
and build an understanding of how it works.
• Play fosters curiosity, creativity, and problem-solving skills. It supports learners’ well-being,
resilience, motivation and engagement & prepares learners for life- long learning.
Project Based Learning
• Learners gain knowledge and skills by working for an extended period of time to investigate
and respond to authentic, engaging and complex tasks, questions, problems or challenges.
• Learners drive their own learning through inquiry, as they work collaboratively to research and
create projects that reflect their innate potential and talents.
Blended Learning
Involves integrating traditional face-to-face instruction with technology.
Cooperative learning
Involves learners working in small groups collaboratively to accomplish assigned tasks.
Design-based learning (DBL)
Entails the use of open ended, hands -on and challenging experiences that allow learners to apply
theoretical knowledge to develop new ways of solving real-life problems.
Experiential learning
This is learning through reflection, where Learning Experiences are structured and learners take
initiative, make decisions and are accountable for the results. Examples include field trips and
excursions.
OVERVIEW OF PREVOCATIONAL LEVEL
PREVOCATIONAL LEVEL CURRICULUM
The specialised curriculum at the prevocational level, which is predominantly skill- based,
prepares learners with disabilities for basic work skills. At this level, learners are introduced to the
pre-requisite skills in various vocational skill areas to enable them to identify their abilities and
interests in a given field.
The Prevocational Level curriculum designs have been developed for the following categories of
learners with special needs; learners with Intellectual Disability, Deafblindness, Severe Autism,
Severe Cerebral Palsy and Multiple Disabilities.
Categories of Learners at Prevocational Level
Learners with Intellectual disabilities
These are learners with significant subaverage general intellectual functioning existing concurrently
with deficits in adaptive behaviour and manifested during the developmental period that adversely
affects the learner’s educational performance. Learners with intellectual disabilities are classified
into four major categories. These are learners with:
• Mild Intellectual Disabilities
• Moderate Intellectual Disabilities
• Severe Intellectual Disabilities
• Profound Intellectual Disabilities
Characteristics of learners with intellectual disabilities
● Slowness in learning due to delayed rate of intellectual development.
● Being unnecessarily slow in carrying out tasks.
● Learning and memory capabilities are significantly below average in comparison to peers
without disabilities.
● Are deficient in relating information to new situations
● Not able to understand what is said or follow instructions.
● Having trouble focusing on relevant stimuli in learning and in real life situations.
● Having difficulty in both learning and applying skills for a number of reasons, including a
higher level of distractibility, inattentiveness, failure to read social cues, and impulsive
behaviour.
● Having delayed speech, language comprehension and formulation difficulties.
● Failing to develop social and emotional relationships
● Having retarded motor development.
● Lacking rhythm in movement
● Having difficulties in remembering experiences or things learnt.
● Lacking motivation.
● Excessive drooling
● Having excessive purposeless movements
● Having difficulty in paying attention or focusing on an activity to its completion.
● Having difficulty in seeing the consequences of their actions.
● Have slow cognitive processing time.
● Have limited self-care skills and independent living skills
Learners with Deafblindness
These are learners with concomitant visual and hearing impairments, the combination of which
causes such severe communication and other developmental and education needs.
Categories of Learners who are deafblind
Learners with deafblindness are of four categories:
• Congenitally deafblind.
• Congenitally deaf with acquired blindness
• Congenitally blind with acquired deafness.
• Adventitiously deafblind (Aquired Deafness and Aquired Blindness).
General Characteristics of learners who are deafblind
● Difficulty communicating or an inability to communicate in a meaningful way.
● Have a distorted perception of the world.
● Have difficulty in establishing and maintaining interpersonal relationships information from
the surrounding.
● Have medical problems that lead to serious developmental delays.
● Presence of a combined vision and hearing losses
10
● Tactile sensitivity and resistance to being touched.
● Delays in motor development.
● Difficulty following a conversation
● Appear to be withdrawn and isolated
● May be deprived of many of the most basic extrinsic motivations
● Self-stimulatory behaviours resulting from sensory deprivation, isolation, frustration,
confusion and fear.
● Have unique learning styles.
● Difficulty in generalizing information learned to other settings.
● Feeding difficulties and or unusual sleeping patterns.
● May have difficulty anticipating what is going to happen. Clues from the environment or from
the faces/actions of others may be difficult to read.
● Difficulty navigating the environment
Learners with Autism spectrum disorders (ASDs)
Autism spectrum disorders are neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by an impairment in
social reciprocity, atypical communication, and repetitive behaviours. Learners with ASDs often
have difficulties with social communication and interaction, and restricted or repetitive behaviors
or interests. Further, they may also have different ways of learning, moving, or paying attention.
Characteristics of learners with Autism spectrum disorders
● Lines up toys or other objects and gets upset when order is changed.
● Repeats words or phrases over and over (echolalia).
● Plays with toys the same way every time.
● Is focused on parts of objects (for example, wheels).
● Gets upset by minor changes.
● Has obsessive interests.
● Tendency toward following certain routines routine.
● Difficult time with social interactions.
● Stereotyped movements such as flaps hands, rocks body, or runs/spins self in circles, flipping
light switches, hand waving, toe walking.
● Has unusual reactions to the way things sound, smell, taste, look, or feel.
● Delayed language skills.
● Delayed movement skills.
● Delayed cognitive or learning skills.
● Hyperactive, impulsive, and/or inattentive behaviour.
● Has epilepsy or seizure disorder.
● Unusual eating and sleeping habits.
● Gastrointestinal issues (for example, constipation)
● Unusual mood or emotional reactions.
11
● Anxiety, stress, or excessive worry.
● Lack of fear or more fear than expected.
Learners with Severe Cerebral palsy (CP)
Cerebral palsy is a disorder of movement and posture that is caused by a nonprogressive
abnormality of the immature brain that affect the learner’s ability to move and maintain balance
and posture. Learners with Cerebral Palsy are classified into four major categories. These are
learners with;
• increased muscle tone/ stiff muscles (Spastic Cerebral Palsy)
• abnormalities in muscle tone that involve the whole body/ uncontrollable movements
(Dyskinetic Cerebral Palsy.)
• abnormalities of voluntary movement involving balance and position of the trunk and
limbs in space/ poor balance and coordination (Ataxic Cerebral Palsy.)
• more than one type of cerebral palsy/ more than one type of motor pattern is present
(Mixed Cerebral Palsy.)
General characteristics of learners with severe cerebral palsy
● Stiff muscles and exaggerated reflexes (spasticity)
● Variations in muscle tone, such as being either too stiff or too floppy
● Stiff muscles with normal reflexes (rigidity)
Lack of balance and muscle coordination (ataxia)
● Tremors or jerky involuntary movement
● Slow, writhing movements
● Difficulty walking
● Difficulty with fine motor skills
● Difficulty speaking
● Excessive drooling or problems with swallowing
● Intellectual disabilities
● Delayed growth, resulting in smaller size than would be expected
● Presence of Seizures (epilepsy)
● Difficulty hearing (deafness)
● Problems with vision and abnormal eye movements
● Abnormal touch or pain sensations
● Bladder and bowel problems, including constipation and urinary incontinence
Learners with Multiple disabilities.
These are learners who have a combination of disabilities. For example, some learners have a
sensory disability with autism, intellectual and/or physical disabilities.
12
General characteristics of learners with multiple disabilities
● Appear to be withdrawn and isolated
● Have difficulty in establishing and maintaining interpersonal relationships
● Have limited self-care skills and independent living skills
● Have medical problems that leads to serious developmental delays.
● Are defensive of being touched.
● Have feeding difficulties and or unusual sleeping patterns.
● May display an immature behavior inconsistent with chronological age.
● May exhibit an impulsive behavior and low frustration level.
● May execute self-injurious behavior.
● Limited speech or communication.
● Difficulty in basic physical mobility.
● Trouble generalizing skills from one situation to another.
● Need for support in major life activities.

LEARNER CENTRED PEDAGOGIES FOR PREVOCATIONAL LEVEL
Pedagogy refers to sets of learning experiences that facilitate achievement of specific learning
outcomes. Some of the learner centred pedagogical approaches for Prevocational level include:
a)     Task Analysis
● Involves breaking down of concepts into smaller, manageable steps to make learning
more achievable.
b)    Diagnostic Prescriptive Instruction approach
● Emphasises assessing (diagnosing) the learners' individual learning needs and
providing adapted instruction (prescribing) to address those specific needs.
● This approach is highly learner-centred and focuses on understanding learners'
strengths and weaknesses to create targeted interventions for improvement.
c)     Multisensory Approach
13
● This involves incorporating visual, auditory, tactile and kinesthetic elements into the
instruction during learning. It also employs use of gestures, facial expressions, and
tactile cues to convey meaning and pairing spoken language with corresponding signs
or tactile representations to reinforce comprehension.
d)    Differentiated learning
● This is an instructional approach that tailors learning strategies, content, and
assessments to accommodate the diverse needs, skills, interests, and learning styles of
learners. Its goal is to ensure that all learners, regardless of their abilities or
backgrounds, have access to the same educational opportunities and can achieve their
highest potential. Differentiation can be applied in various areas of instruction,
including content, process, product, and learning environment.
e)     Modelling
● Modelling is a teaching strategy where the teacher demonstrates a task, skill, or concept
for the learners to observe and imitate. It involves the teacher showing how to perform
a task or solve a problem step-by-step while providing clear, direct examples of the
desired behaviors, tasks, or learning outcomes for learners to observe and imitate.
f)      Tactile Communication and feedback
● Involves using tactile Sign Language, hand-under- hand guidance, or tactile cues
depending on the individual needs of the learner.
● Learners are provided with meaningful touch cues to convey information and reinforce
learning.
g)     Routines
● Involves creating a structured, predictable sequences of activities or behaviours that are
consistently followed in the learning environment and communicating changes on time.
● Routines are integral to creating a structured and safe classroom atmosphere and helps
learners to anticipate what comes next and engage more fully.
● Routines provide stability and a sense of security, which can significantly reduce
anxiety and improve focus.
h)    Repetition
● This refers to the practice of repeatedly presenting information, instructions, tasks, or
activities to help learners gain mastery over them. It provides learners with additional
opportunities to practice and reinforce concepts until they are understood and can be
performed independently.
i)   Picture Exchange Communication System (PECS)
● This is an augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) approach used to
support learners with communication difficulties, particularly those with autism
spectrum disorder (ASD) and other developmental disabilities. PECS utilises pictures
or symbols to help students express their wants, needs, and ideas when verbal
communication is limited or absent. PECS empowers learners to communicate more
effectively, increasing their social interaction, independence, and overall quality of life.
j)      Inquiry Based Learning
● Learners construct knowledge and meaning from their own experiences.
14
● Learners are engaged in questioning, reasoning and experiential (hands-on activities)
k)    Problem-Based Learning (PBL)
● Learners are involved in solving authentic, open-ended, structured, real-world
problems.
● Learners are engaged in extended processes of asking questions, finding resources and
applying learnt information.
l)      Play Based Learning
● Employs play as the primary means for learners to explore the world, investigate its
properties and build an understanding of how it works.
● Play fosters curiosity, creativity, and problem-solving skills. It supports learners’ well-
being, resilience, motivation and engagement and prepares learners for life-long
learning.
● Play improves coordination, motor and social skills.
m)   Project Based Learning
● Learners gain knowledge and skills by working for an extended period of time to
investigate and respond to authentic, engaging and complex tasks, questions, problems
or challenges.
● Learners drive their own learning through inquiry, as they work collaboratively to
research and create projects that reflect their innate potential and talents.
n)    Blended Learning
● Involves integrating traditional face-to-face instruction with technology.
● Encourages incorporating use of assistive technology tools and software that can
support  the different categories learners  in their learning
o)     Design-Based Learning (DBL)
● Entails the use of open-ended, hands-on and challenging experiences that allow
learners to apply theoretical knowledge to develop new ways of solving real-life
problems.
● It encourages active learning through pursuing individual learner’s interests, providing
a real-world context to learning, while providing intrinsic motivation.
p)    Cooperative learning
● Involves learners working in small groups collaboratively to accomplish assigned tasks.
q)    Experiential Learning
● This is learning through active engagement with materials. Experiential learning helps
learners to gain practical skills, develop critical thinking skills, problem-solving
abilities and positive attitudes and help to enhance their communication and
collaboration skills. This type of learning can take many forms, including hands-on
activities, simulations, group projects, field trips, apprenticeships that allow learners to
apply theoretical knowledge to real-world experiences.

Introduction
This session guides participants to identify and interpret the components of the curriculum design
for effective implementation of CBC.
By the end of the session, the participant should be able to:
a) Identify the components of the curriculum designs for effective implementation.
b) Interpret the curriculum designs for effective implementation of learning.
a) Participants peruse through extracts of curriculum designs to identify the components of
curriculum designs.
b) Participants discuss the various components of curriculum designs with emphasis on how
they are interrelated and developed and make presentations in plenary.
Facilitators Notes
Components and interpretation of the curriculum design
The following are the components of a curriculum design and how they are interpreted in CBC.
● National Goals of Education
● Level learning outcomes
● Essence statement
● Subject general learning outcomes
● Strands and sub strands
● Specific learning outcomes
● Suggested learning experiences
● Suggested Key Inquiry Question(s)
● Core competences
● Pertinent and Contemporary Issues
● Values
● Link to other subjects
● Suggested Non-formal activity to support learning
● Suggested learning resources
● Suggested assessment methods
● Suggested assessment rubric
● Community Service Learning
16
National goals of education
These are the goals that the country has set to achieve through provision of accessible, quality and
relevant education. Kenya has eight national goals that should be achieved through education.
Level learning outcomes
These are demonstrable attributes that are expected in a learner after completing a given level of
education, for example middle school education or Prevocational level.
Essence Statement
An essence statement gives a general overview of a subject. It summarises the fundamental ideas of
each subject. It also explains the rationale and justification of inclusion of the subjects in the
curriculum
Strand and Sub Strand
● A strand is a broad area of study within a specific subject. It is a consistent phenomenological
idea or concept that runs through the subject.
● A strand also cuts across all levels of education.
● A sub-strand represents smaller concepts within the strand.
Learning outcomes
They are the end result of what the learner is able to demonstrate upon completion of a lesson, sub -
strand, strand, subject or level.
Categories of learning outcomes
i) Level learning outcomes
These are the demonstrable end results expected in learners after having gone through a specific
level of CBC education. For example, Early Years, Middle School Education and Senior School
Education. They are stated in general terms.
ii) General learning outcomes
These learning outcomes indicate what the learner is expected to achieve in a given subject
iii) Specific Learning Outcomes
Specific learning outcomes indicate the expected observable changes in the learner after covering
a sub -strand or a lesson. They specify what the learner should know, is able to do and
demonstrate after participating and completing a given sub-strand or lesson.
• Outcomes are usually expressed through the application of knowledge, skills and attitudes.
Specific learning outcome should have the following components:
• The action verb (the verb represents the three domains of learning including knowledge,
skills and attitudes).
• The object of the verb (the outcome should also have an object, which answers the question
“what”).
• The context (the outcome also has a context, which answers the questions “why”, “where”,
‘’how” and “when”).
17
Suggested learning experiences
Learning experiences comprise of activities that the learner is engaged in during the lesson. The
activities may be carried out by an individual learner or as a group work activity. However, they
should ultimately enable the learner to achieve the intended specific learning outcomes of the lesson.
Learning experiences enable the learner to:
• Acquire knowledge, skills and develop attitudes
• Acquire the intended competences
• Acquire values, pertinent and contemporary issues
• Learn from one another
• Self-regulate and evaluate
• Engage deeply in the subject matter
• Reflect on the learning process
• Interact with others during the learning process
Key Inquiry Question(s)
Key Inquiry Question(s) (KIQ) is an approach where the teacher uses questions to prod learners
thinking to allow them to create information using their own words and understanding. They;
• help to focus the learning,
• probe for deeper meaning and set the stage for further questioning,
• foster the development of critical thinking skills and higher order capabilities such as
problem solving,
• allow learners to explore ideas in an open-ended, non-judgmental, meaningful and
purposeful way,
• encourage collaboration amongst learners, teachers, and the community and integrate
technology to support the learning process.
Writing Key Inquiry Question(s)
Consider the focus of your learning outcome and the sub strands as given in the curriculum design
Core Competencies to be developed
A competency is the ability to apply appropriate knowledge, skills, attitudes and values to
successfully perform a task. Core Competencies are sets of intellectual, personal, social and
emotional proficiencies that students should develop in order to engag e in deep, lifelong
learning. The core competencies are developed through exposing the learner to stimulating
learning experiences. The learning areas serve as vehicles through which the core competencies
are developed over time.
The seven core competencies to be developed are:
• Communication and collaboration
• Critical thinking and problem solving
• Imagination and creativity
• Digital literacy
• Citizenship
• Learning to learn and
• Self-efficacy.
18
VALUES
These are principles, qualities ,  beliefs or standards that guide an individual  to respond or
behave in a given circumstance or situation.Values influence how we feel, act and make
choices in life. Nurturing of values will facilitate the achievement of moulding ethical citizens.
Values are intended to address the prevailing societal challenges and usher in a desirable future.
The eight core values which have been mainstreamed in CBC are:
▪ Love
▪ Responsibility
▪ Respect
▪ Unity
▪ Peace
▪ Patriotism
▪ Social Justice
▪ Integrity
Values  should be mainstreamed through the whole  school approach. Mainstreaming is the
process of identifying suitable opportunities in specific learning areas, where values can be
incorporated in the learning experiences.
PERTINENT AND CONTEMPORARY ISSUES (PCIS)
PCIs are salient issues that have the potential to affect learner’s psychosocial wellbeing,
access to education, retention, transition, completion and ultimately advancement in the
world of work. Education is supposed to equip learners with cognitive and psychosocial
competencies and values necessary in addressing challenges of everyday life.
The PCIs mainstreamed in the learning areas are in four categories:
1. Citizenship: Peace education, Integrity, Ethnic and racial relations, Social cohesion,
Patriotism and Good governance, Child’s rights, Child care and protection.
2. Health Promotion: HIV and AIDS, Alcohol and Substance use, Life style diseases,
personal hygiene, Prevention of Communicable and non communicable diseases,
Menstrual Disorders prevention among others.
3. Life Skills Education, Moral Education and human sexuality Education.
4. Social –economic Issues: Environmental Education, Disaster Risk Reduction ,Safety &
security, radicalization & terrorism prevention education, child care & protection, Gender
and Animal Welfare Education and indigenous knowledge.
19
Link to other subjects/ learning areas
This refers to the relationship between two or more subjects/learning areas. It is a conscious
effort to use learning of concepts in one subject/learning area to relate to learning of concepts
in another subjects/learning area. This requires integration of  learning to enable the learner to
make connections across strands and sub strands of different subjects/learning areas. The
teacher should also use related concepts in other subjects/learning areas to reinforce concepts
in the given subjects/learning area. The awareness of linkages between subjects/learning areas
gives an opportunity to borrow and share learning resources in different subjects/learning areas,
thus optimising on available resources.
Suggested Learning Resources
These are any materials, tools and persons that teachers and learners use to facilitate learning
and understanding of concepts. Learning resources make learning real, practical and
pleasurable for the learners.
Suggested Assessment methods
Assessment methods are the strategies and procedures of collecting information to determine
the extent to which learners demonstrate achievement of the specified learning outcomes.
The main purpose of assessing learners is to:
● Inform learning decisions
● Establish the level of learner’s competence
● Ascertain progress against the learning outcomes
● Encourage learners to make judgments about their performance
● Enhance learner motivation
● Identify where intervention, focused support or referral is required
● Make decisions regarding choice of subject, course and careers pathways.
Some of the assessment method include:
● Written assignment
● Observation,
● Oral questioning
● Peer assessment
● Self-assessment
● Project work
Assessment rubric

By the end of the sub strand, the learner should be able to;

LEARNING EXPERIENCES:
Guide learners individually, in purposive pairs or groups to:
• Observe and discuss virtual or actual samples to locate the place values of specific digits in a decimal
number from the place value chart. Learners with manipulation difficulties could be assisted by peers or
use assistive technology to perform the task. Learners with speech difficulties could use Augmentative
and Alternative modes of Communication. Communication and collaboration will be developed as the
learners work in pairs or groups to identify the place value and total value of decimal numbers. Inquiry
based learning may be used as learners observe and discuss virtual or actual samples to locate the
place values of specific digits in a decimal number from the place value chart.
• Work out the place value of digits in decimal numbers using place value apparatus and worksheets.
Problem based learning as learners work out the place value of digits in decimal numbers using place
value apparatus and worksheets. Unity is enhanced as the learner cooperates and works harmoniously
with peers to find the place value of digits in decimal numbers.
• Use adapted ICT devices to learn more about place value of digits in decimals. Learners with lower
extremities could be provided with footboards for tablets/ keyboards. Adjust light/ glare on the screens
of the digital devices appropriately for learners who are sensitive to light. Digital literacy is enhanced as
learners use digital devices in searching. Responsibility and integrity is nurtured as they operate the
digital devices.  Cooperative learning could be used during group activities as learners use ICT devices
to learn more about place value of digits in decimals.
ASSESSMENT METHODS:
• Observation - during observation the teacher should consider learners functional ability.
• Oral questions - learners with speech difficulties could use alternative modes of communication to
respond. They could also be given more time to respond.
• Written test -learners with manipulation difficulties could use adapted writing tools or assistive devices
to type their response. They could also answer the questions orally as they are recorded or be supported
by a scribe to write their responses. In addition, they could be given additional time.

Place value charts of appropriate size to enable easy manipulation, Number cards of appropriate size,
worksheets, Abacus, course book, adapted digital devices, adapted writing tools such heavy gauge paper,
universal cuffs, book holders

and charts on process of diffusion.
● Time: Adequate time should be allocated during the assessment to allow learners undertake the
assessment.
● Response: Learners should be allowed to respond to assessment in the most suitable way. For
example, learners who challenges with writing and reading be provided with scribes.
● Assessment tools: Appropriate assessment tools should be utilized depending on the assessment
task. For example, a rubric can be used in assessment this lesson.

Essence of Christian Religious Education
 Christian Religious Education endeavours to equip the learner with
knowledge, skills, values and attitudes for holistic development.
 The values include; love, chastity, kindness, generosity, obedience, respect,
responsibility, integrity, patience, and perseverance.
 CRE seeks to produce a competent learner with good Christian character,
able to cope with challenges in daily life.
 This is in line with the National Goal of Education number (IV) which states
that education should promote sound moral and religious values.

Transformative Learning Approaches
The main methodology in the teaching and learning of CRE is:
1. Life approach; this implies that, the teacher begins the lesson by exploring the
learner’s day-to-day experiences and guides them to discover the religious significance
of their experiences in relation to the Christian faith.
This resonates with Jesus’ Catechetical approach
Jesus’ model begins with what is known and proceeds to divine revelation and comes
back to practical implications. He used the following methods: Story telling, parables,
wise sayings, word pictures, experiential learning, questions and answers. The
audience/disciples responded through critical reflection and response. Jesus Christ is
the greatest Educator who ever lived.
The Moral Construction Approach
Advocated by Piaget and Kohlberg that learners can derive morality by social
interaction and principled reasoning in a classroom situation.
Blended Learning
• Blended learning is integrating traditional face-to-face instruction with
technology.
• The Blended learning environments extend the reach of the instruction
beyond the classroom using digital resources,
• Some portion of the learning occurs online, with the learner being able to
manage the pace at which they learn,
• The other portion of the learning is teacher-led, usually conducted through
webinars, allowing remote learners to engage more easily.
• Blended learning is reportedly more effective than pure face-to-face or pure
online classes.
Collaborative and Cooperative
Learning
 Collaborative learning is based upon consensus building through cooperation by
learners working in groups, in contrast to competition, where  individuals compete
with each other.
 Collaborative learning is more learner cantered in that working together results in
greater understanding than if one had worked independently.
 Cooperative Learning is very similar to Collaborative learning except that it
introduces a more structured setting with the teacher guiding the learning
environment.
 Cooperative learning is thus defined by a set of processes which help learners
interact together in order to accomplish a specific task
Communities of Practice
 Questioning
 Exploring alternatives
 Application
 Reintegrating and grounding of new perspectives
 learners engage in interactive conversations that draw on
personal experiences and religious traditions. They read the Bible
and other relevant resources and listen to each person’s
perspectives, questions, issues and insights and propose
responses, this becomes a learning community of practice geared
towards critical inquiry
Problem-Based Learning (PBL)
 Problem-based learning (PBL) is a student-centred approach where learners
learn about a subject by working in groups to solve open-ended problems.
 The problem is what drives the motivation and the learning.
 PBL is thus an instructional method that initiates learning by creating a need
to solve authentic tasks.
 This method is applicable in CRE as learners discuss, brainstorm, share
experiences and conduct debates in pairs or groups to solve challenges they
face in daily life.
Differentiated Learning
 Differentiation means tailoring instruction to meet individual needs of learners.
 The learning environment, use of continuous assessment and flexible grouping makes
differentiated learning a successful approach to instruction.
 Teachers can differentiate at least four classroom elements based on learner’s readiness,
interest, or learning needs: These are;
1. Content – what the learner needs to learn or how the learner will get access to the
information;
2. Process – activities in which the learner engages in order to make sense of or master
the content;
3. Products – culminating projects that ask the learner to rehearse, apply, and extend
what he or she has learned in a unit; and
4. Learning environment – the way the classroom works and feels.
Inquiry Based Learning
 Inquiry Based learning involves providing learners with experiences that enable
them to develop understanding about aspects of the world around them.
It is based on constructivist learning theories where learners construct knowledge and
meaning from their experiences through the development and use of investigative
skills.
It incorporates a process of exploring the world, which leads to:
a) Asking questions
b) Making discoveries
c) Conducting research/experiments
IBL is rooted in the famous Chines proverb
“Tell Me and I Forget; Teach Me and I May Remember; Involve Me and I Learn”
IBL Cont.…
It involves:
 Field-work
 Case studies
 Investigations
 Individual and group projects
 Research projects is an innovative approach to learning where learners drive
their own learning through inquiry, as they work collaboratively to research
and create projects that reflect their innate potential and talents.

1. Essence statement
Arabic is among the 6 major languages of the world being
recognised by the United Nations (UN) and the African Union
(AU).
 Arabic is spoken by an estimated population of over five
hundred million users. The language has greatly influenced some
local languages like Kiswahili. E.g.
ﻛﺘﺎب-- Kitabu
ﻗﻠﻢ- Kalamu
دﻓ- Daftari
LINK TO SENIOR SCHOOL
At junior school -the Learner is expected to acquire the four
language skills: listening, speaking, reading and writing at a basic
level in the  curriculum. This will give the learner an opportunity
to acquire language competencies in an experiential, innovative
and flexible ways
At senior school-the learner will transit to Senior School
having acquired basic Arabic proficiency.
Organization of Strands and Sub Strands
 Arabic  curriculum  design use themes in learning experiences
as a vehicle to develop the four   language skills(listening skills,
speaking skills , reading skills  and writing skills)
The theme is spiral in nature(progressive)- from Grade 4-9
Grade7-9 Curriculum design  has 9 themes as follows:
(1) Greetings and introduction                       (6) Foods and drinks
(2) Family                                                        (7) My body
(3) My surrounding                                          (8) Weather and
environment
(4) Time                                                            (9) Getting around
(5) Fun and enjoyment
CONT…..
Arabic Grade 7-9 Curriculum design comprises of 3 strands
namely :
(1)Listening and speaking.
(2) Reading  .
(3) Writing.
The grammar is not a stand alone strand  but was embedded in
the 3 strands through out the design.

Here are some of  the Arabic skills learners in Junior
school are  envisaged to achieve :
 Listening and speaking skills: oral presentation, speaking

 Reading skills: reading comprehension, reading fluency,
reading for information, extensive reading, intensive reading.
 Writing skills: Handwriting, mechanics of writing, descriptive
writing, creative writing, functional writing.

SUGGESTED PEDAGOGIES
(1) Communicative Language Learning
(2)Task-Based Learning Method
(3) Problem Based Language Learning-PBL
Other approaches include:
Inquiry based learning-questioning, research
Debate based learning- organised debates
Experiential learning- hands on activities, simulations, group activities, field trips,
narratives, experiments, games, storytelling, surveys.
Cooperative learning- creating messages for the school magazine, chain story telling.
Collaborative learning- group work, pair work, dramatization, role play, hot seating,
discussions, brainstorming, debate.
Reflective learning – making predictions, linking what is read to own experiences,
demonstrations.
Blended learning- using ICT to practice production of speech sound, computer generated
language games

Core Competencies to be developed:
 Communication and Collaboration: This is enhanced as the learner contributes to group discussions when working jointly tosummarise the key ideas from the
recording related to the theme.
 Digital Literacy: This is enhanced as the learner interacts with technology when watching a video presentation and identifying different activities people carry

Learning resources for Arabic
The teaching and learning resources may be categorized as
follows:
1.Visual resources such as text books, posters, pictures, charts
and map.
Audio resources such as audio tapes, audio recorder, radio
broadcasts and phone.
2.Audio-visual resources such as films, video tape, Compact
Disc (CD), computer slides, television broadcasts and interactive
digital content.
3.Other resources such as resource persons, library, museums,
historical sites,  archives and cultural centres.
